intro: Muslims believe God sent many prophets, and the Qur'an tells their stories. Many of them are people the Bible tells about too: Adam, Nuh (Noah), Ibrahim (Abraham), Yusuf (Joseph), Musa (Moses), Maryam (Mary) and Isa (Jesus). In this unit you will read how the Qur'an tells these stories, and you will set them beside the Bible's telling.

You will find a boy in a well, a baby in a basket, a fire that turned cool, and a baby who spoke from the cradle. You will meet the only woman the Qur'an calls by name. And you will learn what the Qur'an says about Muhammad, whom Muslims believe was the last prophet.

By the end you will be able to name the main prophets in the Qur'an, tell what the Qur'an says about each, and compare a Qur'an story with a Bible story. You will practice saying "the Qur'an says" and "Muslims believe," the way people study holy books together with respect.
bigQuestion: What stories does the Qur'an tell about the prophets, and how do Jews, Christians and Muslims each read them?

timeline.t: The Qur'an says God made the first person and taught him the names of all things
The Qur'an says Nuh warned his people, built an ark and was saved from a flood
The Qur'an says Ibrahim broke idols, passed a hard test and built the Kaaba with Ismail
Surah 12 tells Yusuf's story from the well to Egypt to forgiving his brothers
The Qur'an says God spoke to Musa from a fire and parted the sea for his people
Muslims believe God gave the Zabur (Psalms) to Dawud (David)
The Qur'an says Maryam was chosen by God and gave birth to Isa under a palm tree
Muslims believe Isa was a prophet who healed and taught by God's power
Muhammad is born in Mecca, as Muslim tradition tells it
Muslims believe the first words of the Qur'an come to Muhammad
Muslim tradition says Ja'far recites Surah Maryam to the Christian king of Abyssinia
Muhammad dies in Medina; Muslims call him the seal of the prophets

a chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114

the book Muslims believe God gave to Musa; for Jews, the first five books of the Bible
the being who, the Qur'an says, refused to bow to Adam
the great boat Nuh built, in both the Qur'an and the Bible

the square stone building in Mecca that the Qur'an says Ibrahim and Ismail built
the feast of the offering, which remembers Ibrahim's test with his son

test.q: How many prophets does the Qur'an name?
test.why: The Qur'an names 25 prophets; 114 is the number of surahs.

test.q: What does the Qur'an say God taught Adam?
test.why: The Qur'an (2:31) says God taught Adam the names of all things.

test.q: What is one difference between the Qur'an's Nuh story and Genesis?
choices: The Qur'an tells of a son of Nuh who would not board
Genesis says Noah lived in Mecca
test.why: The Qur'an (11:42–43) tells of a son who refused to board; Genesis says all of Noah's sons were saved.

test.q: In the Qur'an, why did Ibrahim break the idols?
choices: To show his people the idols had no power
test.why: The Qur'an (21:58–67) says Ibrahim broke the idols so people would see they could not speak or help.

test.q: Which son does the Bible name in the story of Abraham's test?
test.why: Genesis 22 names Isaac; the Qur'an does not name the son, and most Muslims say Ismail.
Eid al-Adha, the feast of the offering, remembers the day Ibrahim was ready to give up his son.

test.q: Which surah calls itself "the best of stories" and tells one whole story?
test.why: Surah 12, Yusuf, tells Yusuf's whole story in 111 ayahs.

test.q: How does the Qur'an's Yusuf story end?
choices: Yusuf goes back to the well
Yusuf forgives his brothers and the family is together
test.why: Surah 12 ends with forgiveness (12:92) and the family reunited in Egypt.

test.q: Which prophet is named most often in the Qur'an?
test.why: Musa is named more than 130 times; Muhammad only four.

test.q: What does the Qur'an say God gave Musa on the mountain?
test.why: The Qur'an (7:145) says God gave Musa tablets; the calf was made by the people while he was away.

test.q: Who is the only woman named in the Qur'an?
test.why: Maryam (Mary) is the only woman the Qur'an names; Surah 19 is named for her.

test.q: What do Muslims believe about Isa?
choices: He was the Son of God
He was not born of Maryam
He was a prophet and messenger, not God's son
test.why: The Qur'an calls Isa a messenger and the Messiah, son of Maryam, and says God has no son.

test.q: Whom does the Qur'an call "People of the Book"?
test.why: The Qur'an uses this name for Jews and Christians, who have holy books from God.

test.q: What does the Qur'an call Muhammad in 33:40?
test.why: Surah Al-Ahzab 33:40 calls him the seal of the prophets.

test.q: Which is a respectful way to talk about a belief in a public school?
choices: "Muslims believe the Qur'an came from God"
test.why: "Muslims believe" describes a belief without telling anyone what to believe.

write.prompt: Pick one prophet from this unit: Nuh, Ibrahim, Yusuf, Musa or Isa. Answer: How does the Qur'an tell this prophet's story, and how is the Bible's telling alike or different? Cite two or three passages by surah and ayah (for example, 12:92) or by Bible book and chapter (for example, Genesis 22). Explain what each text says and how Muslims, Jews or Christians read it.
tips: Name the text you cite: the surah and ayah, or the Bible book and chapter.
Say "the Qur'an says," "the Bible says," "Muslims believe" or "Christians believe." Do not say which is right.
Find one thing that is the same and one thing that is different in the two tellings.
Use the unit's words: prophet, surah, People of the Book, compare.
End with what you think each book wants its readers to learn.

title: Prophets in the Qur'an

chapters.title: Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim and Yusuf
chapters.bigQuestion: How does the Qur'an tell the stories of the early prophets, and how are they like the Bible's stories?

story.title: Eleven Stars, the Sun and the Moon
story.kicker: A boy has a strange dream, and his father tells him to keep it secret.
paragraphs: A boy wakes up early. He runs to find his father. "Father," he says, "I saw eleven stars in my dream. I saw the sun and the moon too. They were all bowing down to me." His father listens carefully. He does not laugh. He looks worried and proud at the same time.

"My son," the father says, "do not tell your brothers about this dream. They might grow jealous. They might plan something against you." The boy has eleven brothers. His father loves him very much, and the brothers know it. The father thinks the dream means something big is coming.

The boy is Yusuf (Joseph). His father is Yaqub (Jacob). The Qur'an tells this story in Surah 12, a chapter named Yusuf. It calls the story "the best of stories." It is the only long story the Qur'an tells from beginning to end in one surah. Muslims read it in Ramadan and at home.

The Bible tells about Joseph too, in the book of Genesis. In the Bible, Joseph also dreams of eleven stars, the sun and the moon. Jews, Christians and Muslims all know this boy. But each book tells his story in its own way. In this chapter, you will read how the Qur'an tells about Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim and Yusuf.
story.think: Why do you think the father tells Yusuf to keep his dream a secret from his brothers?

lessons.title: What a Prophet Is
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe God sent many prophets to bring people the same message, and the Qur'an names 25 of them.
reading: A *prophet* is a person who brings a message from God. Muslims believe God sent prophets to every people. The Qur'an says that some prophets are named in the book and some are not. It names 25 prophets. Some are called messengers too, because Muslims believe they brought a book or a new law.

Many of the prophets in the Qur'an are people the Bible tells about. The Qur'an gives their names in Arabic. Adam is Adam. Nuh is Noah. Ibrahim is Abraham. Yusuf is Joseph. Musa is Moses. Isa is Jesus. Muslims believe the last prophet was Muhammad.

Muslims believe all the prophets taught one message. The message is that there is one God, and people should worship God and be good. In the Qur'an, God tells the prophets' stories to Muhammad. The Qur'an says the stories are lessons for people who think (12:111, Surah Yusuf).

words.d: a person who brings a message from God; Muslims believe there were many prophets
in Muslim belief, a prophet who brings a book or a new law from God
a chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114

look.title: Surahs Named for Prophets
look.cite: Chapter names and numbers in the standard Qur'an (Cairo edition, 1924)
look.prompt: Which of these surahs comes closest to the front of the book? Which comes near the end?

check.q: What is a prophet, in Muslim belief?
choices: A person who brings a message from God
A king who rules a city
An angel who lives in heaven
check.why: In the Qur'an, a prophet is a person chosen to bring God's message to people.

check.q: How many prophets does the Qur'an name?
check.why: The Qur'an names 25 prophets; 114 is the number of surahs.

check.q: Which name is the Arabic name for Abraham?
check.why: Ibrahim is Abraham; Nuh is Noah, Musa is Moses and Isa is Jesus.

lessons.title: Stories Shared by Three Books
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an, the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Bible tell about many of the same people, each in its own way.
reading: Jews read the *Hebrew Bible*. Christians read the Bible, which has the Old Testament and the New Testament. Muslims read the Qur'an. All three books tell about Adam, Noah, Abraham and Joseph. That is one reason people call Judaism, Christianity and Islam "Abrahamic" faiths.

The books do not tell the stories the same way. The Bible tells a story in order, from start to finish, with many details. The Qur'an usually tells a short part of a story. It often tells the same story in more than one surah. It says what the story teaches.

The Qur'an says that God sent earlier books too. Muslims believe God gave the *Torah* to Musa (Moses). They believe God gave the Gospel to Isa (Jesus). Muslims call Jews and Christians "People of the Book." In this chapter you will compare the tellings.

words.d: the holy book of Judaism; Christians call most of it the Old Testament
the first five books of the Hebrew Bible; Muslims believe God gave a Torah to Musa
the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians, who have holy books too

look.title: Two Ways to Tell a Story
look.text: Imagine two friends tell you about the same soccer game. One tells you every play, from the first kick to the last whistle. The other says, "Our team was losing. Then we kept trying and won. Never give up." The Bible often tells a story the first way. The Qur'an often tells it the second way.
look.prompt: Which way of telling would you use to teach a lesson? Which way would you use to share the whole story?

check.q: Which three religions share stories about Adam, Noah and Abraham?
check.why: Judaism, Christianity and Islam all tell about these figures; that is why they are called Abrahamic faiths.

check.q: How does the Qur'an usually tell a story from the Bible?
choices: In short parts, often in more than one surah
In one long book from start to finish
As a poem with no lesson
check.why: The Qur'an usually tells a short part of a story and says what it teaches; the Bible tells more of the story in order.

check.q: Whom does the Qur'an call "People of the Book"?
check.why: The Qur'an uses "People of the Book" for Jews and Christians, who have holy books.

lessons.title: Adam, the First Person
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says God made Adam, taught him the names of things, and told the angels to bow to him.
reading: The Qur'an says God made Adam, the first person, and made him a *khalifa* on the earth. That word means someone who takes care of something for someone else. God taught Adam the names of all things. Then God told the *angels* to bow to Adam. They bowed (2:30–34, Surah Al-Baqarah).

One being did not bow. His name was *Iblis*. The Qur'an says he was proud. He said he was made of fire and Adam was made of clay. Muslims believe Iblis became Shaytan, the one who whispers to people to do wrong (7:11–18, Surah Al-A'raf).

Adam and his wife lived in a garden. God told them not to eat from one tree. Iblis tricked them, and they ate. They said sorry to God. The Qur'an says God forgave them and sent them to live on the earth (2:35–37; 7:19–25). The Qur'an does not give Adam's wife a name. Muslim tradition calls her Hawwa (Eve).

words.d: a caretaker; the Qur'an says God made Adam a caretaker of the earth
beings Muslims believe God made from light to serve and carry messages
the being who, the Qur'an says, refused to bow to Adam out of pride

look.title: The Angels Bow
look.text: The Qur'an says that God told the angels He was going to put a caretaker on the earth. The angels asked why, since people would do harm. God said, "I know what you do not know." Then God taught Adam the names of all things and told the angels to bow to him.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:30–34, Surah Al-Baqarah (The Cow), told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What does God teach Adam before the angels bow? Why might that matter in the story?

check.q: In the Qur'an, what did God teach Adam?
check.why: The Qur'an (2:31) says God taught Adam the names of all things; the boat belongs to Nuh's story.

check.q: Who refused to bow to Adam, according to the Qur'an?
check.why: The Qur'an says Iblis refused out of pride; Jibril is the angel who Muslims believe brought the Qur'an.

check.q: What does the Qur'an say happened after Adam and his wife ate from the tree?
choices: They said sorry and God forgave them
They sailed away in an ark
check.why: The Qur'an (2:37) says Adam turned to God and God forgave him; then they lived on the earth.

lessons.title: Adam in Two Books
lessons.mainIdea: The Bible and the Qur'an both tell about Adam and the garden, but they tell some parts differently.
reading: The Bible tells about Adam in the book of Genesis, chapters 2 and 3. There, a snake tells Eve to eat from the tree. Eve eats first and then gives some to Adam. God sends them out of the garden. Many Christians read this as the start of sin for all people.

The Qur'an tells the story in a shorter way. It says Shaytan whispered to both of them. It does not say the wife ate first. It says they both did wrong, both said sorry, and God forgave them. Most Muslim readers say each person is responsible for their own deeds, not for Adam's.

Both books agree on a lot. Both say God made Adam. Both tell about a garden and a tree. Both say the first people did wrong. When you *compare* two tellings, look for what is the same and what is different. Then ask what each book wants its readers to learn.

words.d: the first book of the Bible; it tells about Adam, Noah, Abraham and Joseph
to look at two things and find what is alike and what is different

look.title: Side by Side: The Garden
look.text: Genesis 3 says: a serpent speaks to the woman; she eats and gives to the man; God sends them out of the garden. The Qur'an (2:35–37; 7:20–23) says: Shaytan whispers to them both; they both eat; they both say they did wrong; God forgives them and sends them to live on the earth.
look.prompt: Name one thing the two tellings share and one thing that is different.

check.q: Where does the Bible tell the story of Adam?
check.why: Genesis, the first book of the Bible, tells about Adam; Surah Al-Baqarah is in the Qur'an.

check.q: In the Qur'an's telling, who is tricked into eating from the tree?
check.why: The Qur'an says Shaytan whispered to both, and both ate and both asked forgiveness.

check.q: What is one thing both the Bible and the Qur'an say about Adam?
choices: He was a king of Egypt
He lived in a garden with a tree he was told not to eat from
check.why: Both books tell about a garden and a forbidden tree; the ark is Noah's story and the eleven sons belong to Yusuf's father.

lessons.title: Nuh and the Ark
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says Nuh warned his people for a long time, built an ark, and was saved from a flood with those who believed.
reading: The Qur'an tells about *Nuh* (Noah) in many surahs. One whole surah, Surah 71, is named Nuh. The Qur'an says Nuh told his people to worship one God. He warned them for a very long time. The Qur'an says he stayed among them 950 years (29:14, Surah Al-Ankabut). Most of them laughed at him.

God told Nuh to build an *ark*, a big boat. The Qur'an says people made fun of him while he built it. Then the flood came. Nuh took pairs of animals and the people who believed with him. The Qur'an says one of Nuh's sons would not get in. He said he would climb a mountain. The water covered him (11:36–43, Surah Hud).

The Qur'an says the ark came to rest on a mountain called Judi (11:44). The Bible tells about Noah in Genesis, chapters 6 to 9. In the Bible, the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat, and all of Noah's sons are saved. The Qur'an adds the son who would not believe. It uses the story to teach that each person must choose.

words.d: the prophet Noah; the Qur'an says he built an ark and was saved from a flood
a very large boat; in both the Bible and the Qur'an, Noah builds one
water that covers the land; both books tell about a great flood in Noah's time

look.title: The Son Who Would Not Board
look.text: The Qur'an says the ark sailed on waves like mountains. Nuh called to his son, who stood apart, "My son, come aboard with us." The son said he would climb a mountain to keep safe from the water. Nuh said that nothing could keep anyone safe that day but God's mercy. Then a wave came between them.
look.cite: Qur'an 11:42–43, Surah Hud, told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What does the son think will save him? What does Nuh say will save people?

check.q: Which surah is named for Nuh?
check.why: Surah 71 is named Nuh; Surah 12 is Yusuf and Surah 19 is Maryam.

check.q: What does the Qur'an say Nuh did for a very long time before the flood?
choices: Warned his people to worship one God
check.why: The Qur'an says Nuh warned his people for many years; smashing idols is Ibrahim's story.

check.q: What is one difference between the Qur'an's Nuh story and the Bible's Noah story?
choices: The Qur'an tells of a son who would not board and was lost
The Bible says Noah was a prophet in Mecca
check.why: The Qur'an (11:42–43) tells about a son of Nuh who refused to board; Genesis says all of Noah's sons were saved.

lessons.title: Ibrahim and the Idols
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says Ibrahim broke his people's idols to show they had no power, and God kept him safe from the fire.
reading: *Ibrahim* (Abraham) is one of the most important prophets in the Qur'an. His father's people prayed to *idols*. Idols are statues that people treat as gods. The Qur'an says Ibrahim asked them why. The idols could not hear, see or help them (21:52–67, Surah Al-Anbiya).

One day, the Qur'an says, Ibrahim broke all the idols but the biggest one. When people asked who did it, he said, "Ask the big one!" They knew the idol could not talk. Ibrahim wanted them to see that the idols had no power. The people got angry and threw him into a fire.

The Qur'an says God told the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim, and he was not hurt (21:69). The Bible does not tell this story. But old Jewish stories, called midrash, tell of Abraham breaking idols too. The Qur'an calls Ibrahim a *hanif*, a person who turned to the one God and away from idols.

words.d: the prophet Abraham; the Qur'an calls him a friend of God
a statue or object that people pray to as a god
the Qur'an's word for a person who turns to the one God and away from idols

look.title: Ask the Big One
look.text: The Qur'an says Ibrahim broke the idols into pieces, all but the biggest one. When the people asked who had done this, Ibrahim said the big one had done it, and told them to ask the idols if they could speak. The people looked at each other and knew that the idols could not speak.
look.cite: Qur'an 21:58–65, Surah Al-Anbiya (The Prophets), told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What did Ibrahim want the people to notice about their idols?

check.q: What is an idol?
choices: A statue people pray to as a god
check.why: An idol is a statue or object treated as a god; the Qur'an says Ibrahim's people prayed to idols.

check.q: In the Qur'an, what happened when Ibrahim was thrown into the fire?
choices: The angels put it out with rain
God made the fire cool and safe for him
check.why: The Qur'an (21:69) says God told the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim.

check.q: Does the Bible tell the story of Abraham breaking the idols?
choices: No; it is in the Qur'an and in old Jewish stories, not in the Bible
Yes, in the Gospel of Luke
check.why: The idol story is in the Qur'an and in Jewish midrash; Genesis 22 tells about Abraham and his son on the mountain.

lessons.title: The Test With His Son
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says Ibrahim dreamed he must give up his son, both agreed to obey God, and God gave a ram in the son's place.
reading: The Qur'an tells about a hard test. Ibrahim dreamed that he must give up his son as an offering to God. He told his son about the dream. The son said, "Father, do what you are told. You will find me patient" (37:102, Surah As-Saffat). They both agreed to obey God.

When Ibrahim laid his son down, God called to him. God said he had already done what the dream asked. The Qur'an says God gave a great animal to offer in the son's place (37:103–107). Muslims believe this shows how much Ibrahim trusted God.

The Qur'an does not say which son it was. Most Muslim scholars say it was *Ismail* (Ishmael), Ibrahim's older son. Some early Muslim scholars said it was Ishaq (Isaac). The Bible, in Genesis 22, names the son as Isaac. Jews and Christians read the story with Isaac. Muslims and Jews and Christians all see it as a story about trust in God.

words.d: the prophet Ishmael, Ibrahim's older son; most Muslims say he was the son in the test
the prophet Isaac, Ibrahim's younger son; the Bible names him as the son on the mountain
something given up to God

look.title: One Story, Two Names
look.text: Genesis 22 says God tells Abraham to take "your son, your only son Isaac" up a mountain. The Qur'an (37:100–111) tells the dream and the test but does not name the son. Right after the story, it says God gave Ibrahim good news of Ishaq. Many Muslim scholars read that to mean the son in the test was Ismail, born before Ishaq. Others have read it differently.
look.prompt: Why might the same story have a different son's name in two books? What does each book keep the same?

check.q: In the Qur'an, how did Ibrahim learn he was to give up his son?
choices: An angel came in the daytime
He read it in a book
check.why: The Qur'an (37:102) says Ibrahim saw it in a dream and told his son.

check.q: What did the son say when Ibrahim told him the dream?
choices: He ran away to the mountains
He said the dream was not true
He said his father should do what he was told, and he would be patient
He asked his brothers for help
check.why: The Qur'an says the son agreed to obey God and told his father he would be patient.

check.q: Which book names the son in the test as Isaac?
check.why: Genesis 22 names Isaac; the Qur'an does not name the son, and most Muslim scholars say Ismail.

lessons.title: Building the Kaaba, and Eid al-Adha
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says Ibrahim and Ismail built the Kaaba, and Muslims remember Ibrahim's test each year at Eid al-Adha.
reading: The *Kaaba* is a square stone building in Mecca. Muslims face it when they pray. The Qur'an says Ibrahim and his son Ismail raised its walls and prayed that God would accept their work (2:127, Surah Al-Baqarah). Muslims believe it is the first house built for worshiping the one God.

Every year, Muslims from around the world go to Mecca for the *hajj*. It is a special trip. Many things they do there remember Ibrahim's family. They walk between two hills. Muslim tradition says Ismail's mother Hajar did that. She was looking for water for her baby.

At the end of the hajj comes *Eid al-Adha*, "the feast of the offering." Muslims everywhere celebrate it, not just in Mecca. Families who can afford it give an animal. They share the meat and give some to people in need. It remembers the day Ibrahim was ready to give up his son. In Chicago, families gather for morning prayers and visit each other.

words.d: the square stone building in Mecca that Muslims face when they pray
the trip to Mecca that Muslims try to make once in their lives
the feast of the offering; a holiday that remembers Ibrahim's test

look.title: A Holiday With a Story Inside
look.text: Picture a morning in a Chicago neighborhood. Families walk to a big hall in new clothes. After prayers, they hug and say "Eid Mubarak," which means "blessed feast." Later, meat is packed in bags. One bag goes to the family, one to friends, and one to people who need food. Every part of the day points back to a story about Ibrahim.
look.prompt: Which part of Eid al-Adha connects to the story of Ibrahim's test? Which part helps other people?

check.q: Who does the Qur'an say built the Kaaba?
check.why: The Qur'an (2:127) says Ibrahim and Ismail raised the walls of the House.

check.q: What does Eid al-Adha remember?
check.why: Eid al-Adha, the feast of the offering, remembers the day Ibrahim was ready to give up his son.

check.q: What do many families do with meat on Eid al-Adha?
choices: Keep all of it at home
Share it and give some to people in need
check.why: Families who give an animal share the meat with friends and with people who need food.

lessons.title: The Well and Egypt
lessons.mainIdea: Surah 12 tells how Yusuf's brothers put him in a well, and how he was carried to Egypt and wrongly put in prison.
reading: Surah 12 is the only surah that tells one story from start to finish. It has 111 ayahs. It begins by calling itself "the best of stories." Then it tells Yusuf's dream, the one you read at the start of this chapter. His father, Yaqub, warned him not to tell his brothers.

The brothers were *jealous*. They asked to take Yusuf out to play. Then they put him in a well. They came home crying and said a wolf ate him. They showed their father Yusuf's shirt with fake blood on it. Yaqub did not believe them. He said, "Patience is beautiful" (12:18).

A *caravan* stopped at the well for water and found Yusuf. They sold him in Egypt to a rich man. Later the man's wife tried to make Yusuf do wrong. Yusuf refused. The Qur'an says his shirt was torn from the back, which showed he was running away. Even so, he was put in prison. The Qur'an does not name the man or his wife. The Bible calls the man Potiphar.

words.d: wanting what someone else has; Yusuf's brothers were jealous of their father's love
a group of people and animals traveling together to trade
waiting calmly through hard times; Yaqub said "patience is beautiful"

look.title: The Best of Stories
look.text: At the start of Surah 12, the Qur'an says that God is telling Muhammad the best of stories by revealing this Qur'an to him. Then Yusuf tells his father he saw eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing to him. His father tells him not to tell his brothers, or they may plot against him.
look.cite: Qur'an 12:3–5, Surah Yusuf (Joseph), told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Who is telling the story to whom, according to the surah's opening?

check.q: What makes Surah 12 different from most surahs?
choices: It tells one whole story from start to finish
check.why: Surah Yusuf is the only surah that tells one long story in order.

check.q: What did the brothers show their father to make him think Yusuf was dead?
check.why: The Qur'an (12:18) says they brought his shirt with false blood on it.

check.q: How did Yusuf get to Egypt in the Qur'an's telling?
choices: He walked there with his father
A caravan found him in the well and sold him there
check.why: The Qur'an (12:19–20) says travelers found him in the well and sold him in Egypt.

lessons.title: Dreams, Prison and the King
lessons.mainIdea: In prison, Yusuf explained dreams, and the king's dream about cows brought him out to save Egypt from hunger.
reading: In prison, Yusuf met two men who had strange dreams. He told them what their dreams meant, and he told them about the one God. One man was set free, as Yusuf said. But that man forgot Yusuf for years, and Yusuf stayed in prison (12:36–42).

Then the king of Egypt had a dream. He saw seven fat cows eaten by seven thin cows, and seven green ears of grain and seven dry ones. Nobody could explain it. The freed man finally remembered Yusuf. Yusuf said there would be seven good years, then seven years of *famine*, when little food grows. He told them to store grain (12:43–49).

Yusuf asked that his name be cleared first. The wife who had lied said the truth: Yusuf had done nothing wrong (12:51). The king made Yusuf the one in charge of Egypt's storehouses. In the Bible, in Genesis 41, Pharaoh has the same dream and Joseph is also put in charge. The Qur'an says "the king"; the Bible says "Pharaoh."

words.d: a time when there is not enough food
a building where grain is kept for later

look.title: Yusuf's Story by the Numbers
rows: Fat cows in the king's dream
look.cite: Qur'an 12:4, 12:43–49 (Surah Yusuf); ayah count from the standard Cairo edition, 1924
look.prompt: Which of these numbers also appears in the Bible's telling of Joseph in Genesis 37 and 41?

check.q: What did Yusuf do for the two men in prison?
check.why: The Qur'an (12:36–41) says Yusuf explained the prisoners' dreams and told them about God.

check.q: What did the king's dream mean, according to Yusuf?
choices: The king would have seven sons
Seven good years, then seven years of famine
check.why: Yusuf said the seven fat and seven thin cows meant seven years of plenty and seven of famine.

check.q: What did Yusuf ask for before he came out of prison?
check.why: The Qur'an (12:50–51) says Yusuf wanted the truth known first; the wife then admitted he had done nothing wrong.

lessons.title: The Brothers Return
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an ends Yusuf's story with forgiveness: he tells his brothers there is no blame on them, and the family is together again.
reading: The famine reached Yusuf's family too. His brothers came to Egypt to buy grain. They did not know the man in charge was Yusuf. He knew them. He told them to bring their youngest brother, Binyamin (Benjamin), next time. When they did, Yusuf found a way to keep Binyamin with him (12:58–79).

At last Yusuf told them who he was. The brothers were afraid. Yusuf said, "There is no blame on you today. May God forgive you" (12:92). He sent his shirt home. When it touched his father's face, Yaqub, who had cried until he could not see, could see again (12:93–96).

The whole family came to Egypt. The Qur'an says Yusuf's parents and brothers bowed to him, and Yusuf said his childhood dream had come true (12:100). The Bible, in Genesis 45 to 47, also tells how Joseph forgave his brothers and brought the family to Egypt. Both books make *forgiveness* the end of the story.

words.d: Benjamin, Yusuf's youngest brother
letting go of anger at someone who did you wrong
when family or friends come together again after being apart

look.title: No Blame Today
look.text: When Yusuf's brothers learned who he was, they admitted they had done wrong. Yusuf answered that there would be no blame on them that day, and asked God to forgive them. He told them to take his shirt and lay it on their father's face, and their father would see again.
look.cite: Qur'an 12:91–93, Surah Yusuf (Joseph), told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Yusuf had the power to punish his brothers. What did he choose instead, and why do you think the Qur'an ends the story this way?

check.q: What did Yusuf say to his brothers when they found out who he was?
choices: There is no blame on you today
He told them to leave Egypt
He asked for his shirt back
check.why: The Qur'an (12:92) has Yusuf forgive his brothers with the words that there is no blame on them that day.

check.q: What happened when Yusuf's shirt touched his father's face?
check.why: The Qur'an (12:96) says Yaqub's sight came back when the shirt was placed on his face.

check.q: How is the ending of the Qur'an's Yusuf story like the ending of the Bible's Joseph story?
choices: Joseph punishes his brothers in both
Joseph goes back to live in the well in both
The family stays apart in both
Joseph forgives his brothers and the family comes to Egypt in both
check.why: Both Surah 12 and Genesis 45–47 end with forgiveness and the family reunited in Egypt.

review.q: How many prophets does the Qur'an name?
review.why: The Qur'an names 25 prophets; 114 is the number of surahs.

review.q: Which surah tells one whole story from beginning to end?
review.why: Surah Yusuf tells Yusuf's story in order, in 111 ayahs.

review.q: According to the Qur'an, who refused to bow to Adam?
review.why: The Qur'an says Iblis refused out of pride.

review.q: What does the Qur'an say happened to the fire when Ibrahim was thrown in?
choices: God made it cool and safe
review.why: The Qur'an (21:69) says God told the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim.

review.q: Where does the Bible tell about Adam, Noah, Abraham and Joseph?
review.why: All four are in Genesis, the first book of the Bible.

review.q: What is one difference between the Qur'an and the Bible about Ibrahim's test?
choices: The Bible names the son as Isaac; the Qur'an does not name him
The Qur'an says the son ran away
review.why: Genesis 22 names Isaac; the Qur'an (37:100–111) does not name the son, and most Muslim scholars say Ismail.

review.q: Who does the Qur'an say built the Kaaba?
review.why: The Qur'an (2:127) says Ibrahim and Ismail raised its walls.

review.q: How does the Qur'an's Yusuf story end?
choices: Yusuf goes back to the well
Yusuf forgives his brothers and the family is together
review.why: Surah 12 ends with forgiveness (12:92) and the family reunited in Egypt.

chapters.title: Musa, Maryam, Isa and Muhammad
chapters.bigQuestion: How does the Qur'an tell about Musa, Maryam, Isa and Muhammad, and what does it say about Jews and Christians?

story.title: A Surah Read to a King
story.kicker: A small group of Muslims stands before a Christian king far from home, and one of them begins to recite.
paragraphs: Muslim tradition tells this story. It is about the year 615. In Mecca, the first Muslims were being treated badly. Muhammad told some of them to cross the sea to Abyssinia, a land in Africa. Today it is Ethiopia. A Christian king ruled there. Muslims call him the Negus. Muhammad said the king was fair and would not let anyone be harmed.

Leaders from Mecca followed them. They brought gifts to the king. They asked him to send the Muslims back. The king wanted to hear both sides. He called the Muslims to his court. He asked, "What is this new religion of yours?"

A man named Ja'far stood up. He was Muhammad's cousin. He said that they used to pray to idols and be unkind. Then God sent a messenger who told them to worship one God, tell the truth, and care for the poor. The king asked if Ja'far had any of the words from God. Ja'far began to recite Surah 19, the surah named Maryam.

The surah tells about Zakariya, about Maryam (Mary), and about the birth of her son Isa (Jesus). The story says the king wept as he listened. He said these words and the words of Jesus came from the same light. He would not send the Muslims back. This story comes from the sira, the Muslim tradition about the Prophet's life. It shows how early Muslims talked about Maryam and Isa with Christians.

In this chapter you will read what the Qur'an says about Musa (Moses). You will read about Maryam, Isa and Muhammad. You will see what the Qur'an says about Jews and Christians, the People of the Book. And you will see how three religions share a line of prophets. You will also see where their beliefs are different.
story.think: Why do you think Ja'far chose the surah about Maryam to read to a Christian king?

lessons.title: A Baby in a Basket
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says Musa's mother put him in the river to save him, and Pharaoh's own family took him in.
reading: *Musa* (Moses) is the prophet named most often in the Qur'an. His name appears more than 130 times. His story is told in many surahs. The Qur'an says that *Pharaoh*, the king of Egypt, was cruel to the Children of Israel, the people of Yaqub. He ordered their baby boys killed (28:4, Surah Al-Qasas).

The Qur'an says God told Musa's mother what to do. When she was afraid, she should put her baby in the river and not worry. God promised to bring him back to her (28:7). She did it. Musa's sister followed the basket along the shore to see where it went.

Pharaoh's family found the baby. Pharaoh's wife said, "Do not kill him. He may be a joy to us" (28:9). The baby would not drink from any nurse. Musa's sister said she knew a family who could feed him. So Musa's own mother got to nurse him, just as God had promised (28:12–13). The Bible tells this story in Exodus 2, where Pharaoh's daughter finds the baby.

words.d: the prophet Moses; the prophet named most often in the Qur'an
the king of Egypt in the stories of Musa and Yusuf
the Qur'an's name for the people of Yaqub (Jacob), also called Israel

look.title: Side by Side: Who Found the Baby?
look.text: Exodus 2 says Pharaoh's daughter came down to the river, saw the basket, and took the baby as her own son. The Qur'an (28:8–9) says Pharaoh's household picked him up, and Pharaoh's wife asked to keep him as a joy for them both. In both books, the baby's sister watches, and his own mother is brought to nurse him.
look.prompt: Which person is different in the two tellings? What stays the same?

check.q: Which prophet is named most often in the Qur'an?
check.why: Musa's name appears more than 130 times, more than any other prophet.

check.q: In the Qur'an, who said the baby Musa should not be killed?
check.why: The Qur'an (28:9) gives these words to Pharaoh's wife; the Bible has Pharaoh's daughter find him.

check.q: What did God promise Musa's mother, according to the Qur'an?
choices: That she would go to Egypt
That Musa would come back to her
That the river would dry up
check.why: The Qur'an (28:7) says God promised to return the baby to her, and he did, as her nursing child.

lessons.title: The Burning Bush and Pharaoh
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says God spoke to Musa from a fire, gave him signs, and sent him with his brother Harun to Pharaoh.
reading: When Musa was grown, the Qur'an says, he left Egypt and lived in Midian for years. One night, traveling with his family, he saw a fire on a mountain. He went toward it. God spoke to him from the fire in a holy valley called Tuwa (20:9–16, Surah Ta-Ha).

God gave Musa two *signs*. His staff turned into a snake, and when he put his hand under his arm, it came out shining white. God told him to go to Pharaoh. Musa asked God to send his brother *Harun* (Aaron) with him, because Harun spoke well (20:17–36).

Musa and Harun went to Pharaoh and told him to let the Children of Israel go. Pharaoh called his magicians. They threw down ropes that looked like snakes. Musa threw down his staff and it swallowed them. The Qur'an says the magicians bowed and believed (20:65–70). Pharaoh would not. The Bible tells this in Exodus 3 to 7.

words.d: in the Qur'an, something that shows God's power; also the word for a verse (ayah)
the prophet Aaron, Musa's brother and helper
a person who does tricks; Pharaoh's magicians threw down ropes that looked like snakes

look.title: Take Off Your Shoes
look.text: The Qur'an says Musa saw a fire and told his family to wait while he went to get a burning stick or find the way. When he came near, a voice called, "Musa! I am your Lord. Take off your shoes, for you are in the holy valley of Tuwa."
look.cite: Qur'an 20:9–12, Surah Ta-Ha, told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Why did Musa first go toward the fire? What did he find instead?

check.q: Where does the Qur'an say God first spoke to Musa?
choices: In a basket on the river
In the valley of Tuwa, from a fire
check.why: The Qur'an (20:12) names the holy valley of Tuwa, where a fire was burning.

check.q: Who did Musa ask God to send with him?
check.why: Musa asked for his brother Harun (Aaron), who spoke well (20:29–32).

check.q: What happened when Musa threw down his staff in front of the magicians?
check.why: The Qur'an (20:69) says Musa's staff swallowed up what the magicians had made.

lessons.title: The Sea and the Mountain
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says God parted the sea for the Children of Israel, and Musa later received God's words on the mountain.
reading: The Qur'an says Musa led the Children of Israel out of Egypt by night. Pharaoh's army chased them to the sea. The people were afraid. Musa said God was with him and would show him the way. God told Musa to strike the sea with his staff. It split, and each side stood like a great mountain (26:61–63, Surah Ash-Shu'ara).

The people crossed on dry ground. Pharaoh's army followed, and the water came back over them. The Qur'an says Pharaoh cried out that he believed, but it was too late (10:90–92, Surah Yunus). The Bible tells the crossing in Exodus 14. Both books make it the moment the people are saved.

Then Musa went up the mountain to meet God. He was gone forty nights. The Qur'an says God gave him *tablets* with teachings on them (7:142–145, Surah Al-A'raf). While he was away, the people made a golden calf and worshiped it. Musa came back angry. Muslims believe God gave Musa the *Torah*. In the Bible, Moses also brings tablets down Mount Sinai.

words.d: flat stones with writing; the Qur'an says God gave Musa tablets with teachings
the book Muslims believe God gave to Musa; for Jews, the first five books of the Bible
a statue of a young cow that the people made and worshiped while Musa was away

look.title: How Often the Prophets Are Named
look.cite: Common counts of names in the Arabic text of the Qur'an; counts vary a little by how they are made
look.prompt: Which prophet is named far more than the others? Why might Musa's story be told so often?

check.q: What does the Qur'an say happened when Musa struck the sea?
choices: It split and each side stood like a mountain
The sea rose over the Children of Israel
check.why: The Qur'an (26:63) says the sea parted and each part was like a great mountain.

check.q: What did the people make while Musa was on the mountain?
check.why: The Qur'an (7:148; 20:85–88) says the people made a calf and worshiped it.

check.q: Which book do Muslims believe God gave to Musa?
check.why: Muslims believe the Torah was given to Musa, the Gospel to Isa, the Psalms to Dawud and the Qur'an to Muhammad.

lessons.title: A Surah Named for Maryam
lessons.mainIdea: Maryam (Mary) is the only woman named in the Qur'an, and Surah 19 tells about her childhood and her son.
reading: *Maryam* (Mary) is the only woman the Qur'an calls by name. Surah 19 is named for her. The Qur'an says her mother promised her baby to God's service before she was born. When the baby was a girl, the mother named her Maryam and asked God to protect her (3:35–36, Surah Al Imran).

The Qur'an says Maryam grew up in a place of prayer. A prophet named *Zakariya* took care of her. Whenever he visited, he found food with her. He asked where it came from. She said it came from God (3:37). Seeing this, Zakariya prayed for a child of his own, and God gave him Yahya (John).

The Qur'an says the angels told Maryam that God had chosen her above the women of the worlds (3:42). Muslims honor Maryam very much. Many Muslim girls are named after her. Christians also honor Mary, and she appears in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke in the Bible. The Bible does not tell the story of Maryam's childhood in the temple.

words.d: Mary, the mother of Isa; the only woman named in the Qur'an
the prophet Zechariah, who cared for Maryam when she was young
a book about Jesus in the Christian Bible; also the book Muslims believe God gave to Isa

look.title: Food From God
look.text: The Qur'an says God accepted Maryam and made her grow up well, and Zakariya took care of her. Each time Zakariya came in to her room, he found food there. He asked, "Maryam, where does this come from?" She said, "It is from God. God gives to whom He will without counting."
look.cite: Qur'an 3:37, Surah Al Imran (The Family of Imran), told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What did Zakariya notice, and what did Maryam say about it?

check.q: Who is the only woman named in the Qur'an?
check.why: Maryam is the only woman named; the others are known from Muslim tradition but not named in the Qur'an.

check.q: Who took care of Maryam when she was young, according to the Qur'an?
check.why: The Qur'an (3:37) says Zakariya cared for her in the place of prayer.

check.q: Which of these stories is in the Qur'an but not in the Bible?
choices: Maryam's childhood in a place of prayer with food from God
check.why: The Bible does not tell of Maryam's childhood in the temple; the Qur'an tells it in 3:35–37.

lessons.title: The Birth of Isa
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an says an angel told Maryam she would have a son, Isa, and that he spoke as a baby to defend her.
reading: Surah 19 tells that Maryam went away by herself to the east. God sent an angel, who looked like a man. She was afraid. He said he was a messenger from God, sent to give her a pure son. Maryam asked how she could have a son, since no man had touched her. The angel said it was easy for God (19:16–21).

The Qur'an says Maryam went far away, and the pain of birth came to her under a *palm tree*. She wished she had died. A voice told her not to grieve. God had put a small stream by her, and if she shook the tree, fresh dates would fall (19:22–26).

She carried the baby back to her people. They were shocked. Maryam did not speak; she pointed to the baby. The Qur'an says the baby *Isa* spoke from the cradle. He said, "I am the servant of God. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet" (19:29–30). The Bible tells of Jesus's birth in Luke 2, in a stable in Bethlehem, with Joseph beside Mary. The Qur'an does not mention Joseph.

words.d: Jesus; Muslims believe he was a prophet born of Maryam
the tree the Qur'an says Maryam rested under when Isa was born
a baby's bed; the Qur'an says Isa spoke while still in the cradle

look.title: Two Birth Stories
look.text: Luke 2 says Jesus was born in Bethlehem, laid in a manger, and shepherds came to see him. Joseph was with Mary. The Qur'an (19:22–33) says Maryam was alone under a palm tree with a stream, and dates fell to feed her. When she came home, her baby spoke to defend her. Both books say the birth was a sign from God and that Mary had no husband when the child was conceived.
look.prompt: Name two things that are different in the two tellings, and one thing both books share.

check.q: In Surah 19, what did the angel tell Maryam?
choices: That she would have a pure son
check.why: The Qur'an (19:19) says the angel was sent to give her a pure son.

check.q: Where does the Qur'an say Isa was born?
choices: Under a palm tree by a stream
check.why: The Qur'an (19:23–25) places the birth under a palm tree; the stable is in Luke's telling.

check.q: What does the Qur'an say the baby Isa did?
choices: Spoke from the cradle, calling himself God's servant
check.why: The Qur'an (19:29–30) says the baby spoke and said he was God's servant and a prophet.

lessons.title: Isa, the Messiah, in the Qur'an
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe Isa was a great prophet who healed and taught by God's power, but not the son of God.
reading: The Qur'an calls Isa the *Messiah*, a son of Maryam, and a messenger of God. It says God gave him the Gospel. The Qur'an says Isa did wonders by God's permission. He healed people who were blind and people with skin disease. He made a bird from clay and it came alive. He brought the dead to life (3:49, Surah Al Imran; 5:110, Surah Al-Ma'idah).

Here Muslims and Christians agree on some things and not on others. Both believe Isa was born of Mary without a father. Both believe he healed and taught. Most Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God and part of a Trinity. The Qur'an says God has no son and is only one (4:171; 112:1–4).

The Qur'an also speaks about the cross. It says the people who tried to kill Isa did not kill him, though it seemed so. It says God raised him up (4:157–158, Surah An-Nisa). Most Muslims read this to mean Isa was not crucified. Christians believe Jesus died on a cross and rose again. These are two different beliefs about the same person. In a public school, we learn what each group believes. We do not decide who is right.

words.d: a title for Isa (Jesus) in both the Qur'an and the Bible; in Arabic, al-Masih
the Christian belief that God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit; the Qur'an rejects a Trinity
put to death on a cross; Christians believe Jesus was crucified, most Muslims believe he was not

look.title: What Each Believes About Isa
look.text: Muslims and Christians both say: Isa was born of Maryam (Mary) without a father; he healed the sick; he taught people about God. Christians say: Jesus is the Son of God; he died on a cross and rose again. Muslims say: Isa was a prophet and messenger, not God's son; God saved him, and he was not killed on the cross.
look.prompt: Sort the sentences: which beliefs are shared, and which belong to just one religion? Use "Muslims believe" or "Christians believe" when you answer.

check.q: What does the Qur'an say Isa did by God's permission?
choices: Healed the blind and raised the dead
check.why: The Qur'an (3:49) lists healing, the clay bird and raising the dead, all by God's permission.

check.q: Which belief do Muslims and Christians share about Isa?
choices: He is the Son of God
He was born of Mary without a father
check.why: Both the Qur'an and the Gospels say Mary had no husband when Isa was conceived; the other statements are held by only one group or by neither.

check.q: What do most Muslims believe about the cross, based on 4:157?
choices: Isa was not killed; God raised him up
Isa died and rose on the third day
check.why: The Qur'an (4:157–158) says they did not kill him and God raised him up; most Muslims read this as Isa not being crucified.

lessons.title: Jews and Christians in the Qur'an
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an calls Jews and Christians People of the Book, praises some, argues with some, and tells Muslims to speak with them kindly.
reading: The Qur'an calls Jews and Christians the *People of the Book*. That means people who were given a holy book from God before the Qur'an. The Qur'an says Muslims may eat the food of the People of the Book. It also allows Muslim men to marry their women (5:5, Surah Al-Ma'idah).

The Qur'an says different things in different places. It praises Jews and Christians who believe in God and do good. It says they will have their reward (2:62). It also argues with some Jews and some Christians about their beliefs. It tells Muslims to argue with the People of the Book only in the best way (29:46, Surah Al-Ankabut).

Scholars say many of these verses came from real events in Medina. Muhammad lived there near Jewish tribes, and he met Christians too. Some verses praise. Some warn. Some are about one group at one time. Muslim scholars have long discussed how to read them together. Today many Muslims, Jews and Christians in Chicago meet to study each other's books.

words.d: the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians, who have a holy book from God
the city where Muhammad lived after leaving Mecca, near Jewish tribes
a person who studies a subject deeply for a long time

look.title: Argue in the Best Way
look.text: The Qur'an tells Muslims not to argue with the People of the Book except in the best way, apart from those who do wrong. It tells them to say, "We believe in what was sent down to us and what was sent down to you. Our God and your God is one, and to Him we submit."
look.cite: Qur'an 29:46, Surah Al-Ankabut (The Spider), told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What does this verse tell Muslims to say about God when they talk with Jews and Christians?

check.q: What does "People of the Book" mean in the Qur'an?
choices: Jews and Christians, who have a holy book from God
check.why: The Qur'an uses the phrase for Jews and Christians, who were given holy books before the Qur'an.

check.q: How does the Qur'an tell Muslims to argue with the People of the Book (29:46)?
check.why: The Qur'an (29:46) says to argue only in the best way and to say that their God and ours is one.

check.q: Why does the Qur'an say different things about Jews and Christians in different places?
choices: Because the pages were mixed up
Because it was written by many people
Because it was written in Hebrew
Because many verses came from different real events, and some praise while some warn
check.why: Scholars say many verses came from events in Medina; some praise, some warn, some are about one group at one time.

lessons.title: One Line of Prophets
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe the prophets from Adam to Muhammad brought one message, and the three religions share many of the same figures.
reading: Muslims believe God sent one message again and again, through many prophets. Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud (David), Isa and Muhammad are all on one line. Muslims believe God gave books to some of them. The Torah went to Musa. The *Zabur* (Psalms) went to Dawud. The Gospel went to Isa. The Qur'an went to Muhammad.

Jews, Christians and Muslims do not agree on where the line ends. Jews honor Abraham, Moses and David, and do not count Jesus or Muhammad as prophets. Christians honor the Hebrew prophets and believe Jesus is more than a prophet. They do not count Muhammad as a prophet. Muslims count them all, and believe Muhammad was the last.

Even so, a *timeline* of the three religions has many of the same names on it. When you study a figure like Abraham or Moses, ask three questions. What does the Hebrew Bible say? What does the Christian Bible say? What does the Qur'an say? Then you can compare without saying which is right.

words.d: the Psalms; Muslims believe God gave this book to Dawud (David)
a line that shows events in the order they happened

look.title: Four Books Muslims Believe God Sent
look.cite: Qur'an 3:3–4 (Surah Al Imran), 4:163 (Surah An-Nisa), 17:55 (Surah Al-Isra); order as Muslim tradition gives it
look.prompt: Which of these books do Jews read? Which do Christians read? Which is read by Muslims only?

check.q: Which book do Muslims believe God gave to Dawud (David)?
check.why: Muslims believe the Zabur, the Psalms, was given to Dawud (4:163).

check.q: Which religion counts Muhammad as a prophet?
check.why: Muslims believe Muhammad was a prophet; Jews and Christians do not count him as one.

check.q: What is a good way to compare a shared figure like Moses?
choices: Decide which book is right first
Ask what each of the three books says, then compare
check.why: Comparing means reading what each book says and noting what is alike and different, without ranking.

lessons.title: The Seal of the Prophets
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe Muhammad was the last prophet, and the Qur'an calls him the seal of the prophets.
reading: Muslims believe *Muhammad* was the last prophet. The Qur'an calls him "the *seal* of the prophets" (33:40, Surah Al-Ahzab). A seal is a stamp that closes a letter. Muslims read this to mean that no prophet comes after him. Muslims say "peace be upon him" after his name.

The Qur'an names Muhammad only four times. It usually speaks to him without his name. It says "O Prophet" or "O Messenger." It calls him a *warner* and a bringer of good news. It calls him a mercy to all the worlds (21:107). Muslims believe the Qur'an came to him over about 23 years. That was from about 610 to 632.

The Qur'an says Muhammad was a person, not an angel, and that he did not know the future. It says he was sent to confirm the books that came before. So Muslims believe the Qur'an, the Torah and the Gospel are all from God. Jews and Christians do not share this belief about the Qur'an. Each group reads the others' books in its own way.

words.d: the prophet Muslims believe received the Qur'an; Muslims believe he was the last prophet
a stamp that closes something; the Qur'an calls Muhammad the seal of the prophets
one of the Qur'an's names for a prophet: a person who warns people to do right

look.title: The Seal of the Prophets
look.text: The Qur'an says that Muhammad is not the father of any man among the believers, but he is the messenger of God and the seal of the prophets, and that God knows all things.
look.cite: Qur'an 33:40, Surah Al-Ahzab (The Clans), told in simple words after Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What does a seal do to a letter? How do Muslims use that picture to explain this verse?

check.q: What does the Qur'an call Muhammad in 33:40?
check.why: Surah Al-Ahzab 33:40 calls Muhammad the messenger of God and the seal of the prophets.

check.q: How many times does the Qur'an name Muhammad?
check.why: Muhammad is named four times; Musa is the one named more than 130 times.

check.q: What do Muslims believe "seal of the prophets" means?
check.why: Muslims read "seal" as closing the line of prophets; Adam, not Muhammad, is the first.

lessons.title: Three Religions, One Timeline
lessons.mainIdea: The prophets of the Qur'an can be placed on one timeline that Jews, Christians and Muslims each read in their own way.
reading: Put the prophets in order and you get a timeline that three religions share. Adam and Nuh come first. Then Ibrahim, whom all three call the father of their faith. Then Musa, who Jews say received the Torah. Then Dawud, whose Psalms Jews and Christians sing. Then Isa, whom Christians follow. Then Muhammad, whom Muslims follow.

Each religion stops at a different place. For Jews, the story of God's prophets is told in the Hebrew Bible. For Christians, it leads to Jesus and the New Testament. For Muslims, it leads to Muhammad and the Qur'an. All three tell many of the same stories about the earlier prophets.

In this unit you read about Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim and Yusuf. You read about Musa, Maryam, Isa and Muhammad. You compared the Qur'an's telling with the Bible's. You learned to say "the Qur'an says" and "the Bible says." You learned to say "Muslims believe" and "Christians believe." That is how people study holy books together with *respect*.

words.d: treating people and their beliefs with care, even when you do not share them
the second part of the Christian Bible, which tells about Jesus and his followers

look.title: The Same Names on a Timeline
look.text: Picture a long line on the wall of your classroom. At the left end is Adam. Then Nuh, Ibrahim, Yusuf, Musa, Dawud. Near the right end, Maryam and Isa. At the far right, Muhammad. A Jewish student, a Christian student and a Muslim student each walk along the line. Each one stops at a different place and says, "Here is where my book ends."
look.prompt: Where would each of the three students stop? Which names would all three point to?

check.q: Which figure do Jews, Christians and Muslims all call the father of their faith?
check.why: All three religions look back to Abraham (Ibrahim), which is why they are called Abrahamic.

check.q: Where does the line of prophets end for Muslims?
check.why: Muslims believe Muhammad was the last prophet, the seal of the prophets.

check.q: Which phrase is a respectful way to describe a belief in a public school?
choices: "You must believe Isa was a prophet"
check.why: Saying "Muslims believe" describes a belief without telling anyone what to believe.

review.q: Which prophet is named more than 130 times in the Qur'an?
review.why: Musa (Moses) is the prophet named most often in the Qur'an.

review.q: In the Qur'an's telling, who asked to keep the baby Musa?
review.why: The Qur'an (28:9) gives the words to Pharaoh's wife; Exodus 2 has Pharaoh's daughter.

review.q: Which surah is named for Maryam?
review.why: Surah 19 is Maryam; 12 is Yusuf and 71 is Nuh.

review.q: What does the Qur'an say happened right after Isa was born?
choices: He spoke from the cradle to defend his mother
He built a place of prayer
review.why: The Qur'an (19:29–30) says the baby spoke; the shepherds are in Luke 2.

review.q: Which belief about Isa do Muslims hold, based on the Qur'an?
choices: He is the Son of God
He was a prophet and messenger, not God's son
He was not born of Maryam
review.why: The Qur'an calls Isa a messenger and the Messiah, son of Maryam, and says God has no son.

review.q: Whom does the Qur'an call "People of the Book"?
review.why: People of the Book are Jews and Christians, who have holy books from God.

review.q: What does the Qur'an call Muhammad in Surah 33:40?
review.why: Surah Al-Ahzab 33:40 calls him the seal of the prophets; the Messiah is Isa's title.

review.q: According to Muslim tradition, what did Ja'far recite to the king of Abyssinia?
review.why: The sira says Ja'far recited Surah Maryam (19), and the Christian king wept.
